title: On the Support Vector Effect in DNNs: Rethinking Data Selection and Attribution

problem.claim: Data subset selection and instance attribution rely on gradient manipulation, but practitioners often use only last-layer gradients for tractability.

gap.claim: Last-layer gradient heuristics can be detrimental because of the Support Vector Effect, and existing methods have limitations.

contributions.claim: Introduces the Support Vector Effect as a max-margin-like behavior in the last layer or layers of DNNs.
Develops RandE for data subset selection and PAE for instance attribution.
Uses SVE to scrutinize last-layer-gradient-based data selection and attribution methods and explain reported pitfalls.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The investigation reports explanations for lack of diversity and temporal performance degradation in existing techniques.
The investigation reports vulnerability of existing methods to basic poisoning attacks.
RandE and PAE often outperform the purported state of the art at a fraction of the cost.

narrative_sequence.summary: Gradient manipulation is central to data subset selection and instance attribution in DNNs.
Last-layer gradient heuristics are used for tractability but can be harmful because of SVE.
The paper introduces SVE and applies it to scrutinize existing methods.
The analysis identifies limitations, explains observed pitfalls, and reports security and simplicity implications.
The paper proposes RandE and PAE as more efficient alternatives.

source_observation.claim: Using only last-layer gradients for tractability can be detrimental because of SVE.

interpretation.claim: Computational shortcuts in gradient-based selection and attribution may alter the behavior being measured.

application.claim: Evaluate whether gradient approximations preserve selection or attribution behavior before adopting them for efficiency.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when last-layer gradients are safe or unsafe across models, tasks, or settings.

source_observation.claim: Simpler alternatives are reported to achieve competitive performance at lower cost.

interpretation.claim: Method complexity may not be necessary for effective data selection or attribution.

application.claim: Include simpler, lower-cost baselines when evaluating complex selection and attribution methods.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the conditions under which RandE or PAE outperform existing methods.

unknowns: Datasets, model architectures, and experimental settings are not specified.
No quantitative metrics or comparison results are provided.
The abstract does not define the mechanisms or formal properties of SVE, RandE, or PAE.
